# Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation

Luis Wiedmann Affiliation: Technical University of Munich, MCML
Affiliation: Helmholtz Munich    Leander Girrbach Affiliation: Technical
University of Munich, MCML Affiliation: Helmholtz Munich    Cordelia
Schmid Affiliation: Inria, École normale supérieure, CNRS, PSL Research
University    Zeynep Akata Affiliation: Technical University of Munich,
MCML Affiliation: Helmholtz Munich

###### Abstract

Agent evaluations increasingly go beyond a single success rate,
reporting metrics such as cost, consistency, and robustness. Yet they
typically treat the agent itself as fixed. In practice, an agent is a
configurable system: users decide what to tell it, how long to let it
run, and which model to use, and each of these choices can change how
well and how consistently it performs. We study these choices on a new
benchmark of four scientific tasks, where a coding agent must find and
correctly operate a published specialist model. We investigate five
parts of the agent’s configuration: task information, reasoning,
self-verification, time budget, and backbone model. We find substantial
run-to-run variability, with approximately 54% of the outcome variance
coming from repeating the same configuration rather than changing it.
Across configurations, the information provided to the agent has the
largest effect, exceeding both time budget and model size, while also
reducing cost and improving calibration. Configuration choices also
interact: additional time helps only when the agent has sufficient
information or a capable enough model to use it. Finally, a
trajectory-based taxonomy of agent behavior reveals that prompting an
agent to verify its answer has little effect on its verification
behavior, whereas providing a dedicated verification tool changes that
behavior substantially. These results suggest that agents should be
evaluated as configurable systems themselves, and that some desired
behaviors are more effectively implemented in the system than requested
through prompting. We release the benchmark and more than 18,000 agent
trajectories¹¹ 1
[https://github.com/lusxvr/rethinking-agent-evaluation](https://github.com/lusxvr/rethinking-agent-evaluation).

## 1 Introduction

When agents are used to solve complex tasks, we care not only about
whether they succeed, but also about how reliably they do so, and about
which parts of their configuration determine capability and reliability.
Recent work broadens what is measured about an agent: [Kapoor et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib1) argue that evaluations should not focus only on
performance, but also account for cost and comparability between
methods. [Rabanser et al. (2026)](#bib.bib2) show that capability gains
do not automatically translate into reliability gains, and argue for a
decomposition of agent reliability into consistency, robustness,
predictability, and safety. It remains less clear how an agent’s
configuration itself shapes these measurements: which of its parts drive
capability and reliability, and how these parts interact.

Scientific workflows are a natural setting to study this. Many
scientific tasks rely on specialist models (trained for a specific
scientific domain or task) that a general-purpose LLM cannot directly
replace, so an agent cannot solve them from its own knowledge. Instead,
it has to find the right model, prepare the input data, and write the
code to run it, and each of these steps can be affected by how the agent
is configured. Published results of these specialist models further
provide reference scores against which the agent’s outcome can be
checked. One example is estimating redshift from galaxy images.
Fine-tuning a multimodal LLM to process galaxy images would be costly,
but specialist models for this task already exist, and an agent can use
them instead. We are interested in _how reliably agents can use such
specialist models_ in scientific workflows, and _what contributes to
their effective use_.

In this paper, we use the following terms: the model (or backbone) is
the LLM itself, with no memory across calls and no ability to act on its
own. An agent wraps a model in a loop that lets it act repeatedly: read
the current state, decide on an action, execute it, observe the result,
and decide again. The agent’s harness is the infrastructure that runs
this loop: it dispatches tool calls and manages the model’s context at
each step, including memory and compression. Fundamentally, an agent is
a system consisting of a model and a harness ([de Macedo,
2026](#bib.bib16); [Paniego and Roy Gosthipaty, 2026](#bib.bib12)),
which is reflected in recent implementations of production coding agents
such as Codex or Claude Code ([Lopopolo, 2026](#bib.bib14); [Young,
2025](#bib.bib13); [Shi et al., 2026](#bib.bib15)).

We systematically evaluate how an agent’s configuration affects how well
it uses specialist models to solve scientific tasks. Concretely, we
study five axes of the agent’s configuration: (1) what information the
agent is given; (2) whether the agent generates reasoning and keeps it
across steps; (3) how strongly the agent is asked to verify its own
answer; (4) how much runtime budget the agent has to solve the task; and
(5) how strong the agent’s backbone model is. By varying these axes on a
new benchmark of four scientific tasks from astrophysics and genomics,
we measure how each one contributes to the agent’s outcome and
reliability, and how they interact. In each task, the agent’s outcome is
compared against the specialist model on an evaluation from its original
paper.

We find that agent outcomes are noisy: about 54% of the score variance
among genuine attempts is run-to-run noise rather than an effect of the
configuration. In our main experiments, the information given to the
agent has the largest effect among the axes, outranking both the budget
and the backbone model. The effect of one axis can also depend on
another: additional budget mainly improves the score when the agent
already has enough information to use it productively. Finally, an
analysis of the agent’s behavior shows that some behaviors, such as
self-verification, are hard for the user to influence directly through
prompting and should instead be shaped by the system’s design.

In summary, our contributions are as follows: (1) We systematically
study how the axes of an agent’s configuration influence its outcome and
reliability, finding that information outranks model and budget. (2) We
create an AI-for-Science (AI4S) benchmark in which the agent has to use
specialist models under controlled conditions. We release the benchmark
and 18,240 agent trajectories with their produced artifacts, enabling
reproducibility and further analysis of agent behavior. (3) We derive a
taxonomy of agent behavior from these trajectories and use it to show
that some behaviors are hard for the user to influence directly and
should instead be shaped by the system’s design.

## 2 Related Work

##### AI for Science.

Recent capability gains in machine learning methods and foundation
models enable a broad range of applications in scientific fields outside
classical computer science ([Jumper et al., 2021](#bib.bib20); [Wang et
al., 2023](#bib.bib21)). Furthermore, the transition from isolated
models to agents has intensified the interest in AI as a scientific
companion or as a scientist itself ([Wei et al., 2025](#bib.bib22);
[Gridach et al., 2025](#bib.bib23); [Xin et al., 2025](#bib.bib24); [Lu
et al., 2026](#bib.bib25)). We organize the field into two focus areas:
*(re-)implementation* ([Starace et al., 2025](#bib.bib27)) and
*discovery* ([Majumder et al., 2025](#bib.bib26)). Works on
(re-)implementation reuse scientific publications or their codebase, and
test how well agents can reproduce the findings, methods, or
implementations ([Wang et al., 2026](#bib.bib3); [Chen et al.,
2025](#bib.bib4); [Kim et al., 2026](#bib.bib5); [Bogin et al.,
2024](#bib.bib28); [Falck et al., 2026](#bib.bib29); [Shen et al.,
2026](#bib.bib30)). In parallel, a growing set of works evaluates
agents’ ability to produce genuinely novel discoveries ([Kirgis et al.,
2026](#bib.bib31); [Artiles et al., 2026](#bib.bib32); [Si et al.,
2025](#bib.bib33); [Zahavy, 2026](#bib.bib34); [Si et al.,
2026](#bib.bib35); [Messeri and Crockett, 2024](#bib.bib36)). Our work
is closer to the first area, i.e., (re-)implementation of existing work.
We propose a coding-focused benchmark that enables the agent to freely
explore, test, and write code to operate given specialist models, while
its outcome is judged against their published performance. This makes
the environment controlled and repeatable, so that the agent’s
configuration can be varied systematically and outcomes can be scored
without manual verification.

##### Agents and Their Evaluation.

As agents ([Wooldridge and Jennings, 1995](#bib.bib38); [Yao et al.,
2023](#bib.bib6)) become more capable, evaluating their
performance ([Chang et al., 2024](#bib.bib37)) becomes more challenging.
Their ability to tackle complex, long-horizon tasks ([Kwa et al.,
2025](#bib.bib40)), potentially through multiple instances ([Cemri et
al., 2026](#bib.bib39)), makes failures and capabilities harder to
accurately estimate and understand, which makes a systematic study
necessary ([Zhu et al., 2025](#bib.bib41); [Miller, 2024](#bib.bib43)).
Multiple works agree that a single success metric is insufficient, and
that capabilities have to be judged both in the context of their task
and in terms of their cost and reliability, broadening what is measured
about an agent ([Liang et al., 2023](#bib.bib42); [Kapoor et al.,
2026](#bib.bib44); [Kapoor et al., 2025](#bib.bib1); [Rabanser et al.,
2026](#bib.bib2)). We complement these works by treating the agent as a
configurable system rather than a fixed model, and study how its
configuration shapes these measurements.

## 3 Agent Evaluation and Benchmark Tasks

In our setting, a single agent has access to a collection of specialist
models, including their weights and pre-built environments (i.e., the
libraries and dependencies required to run them). Given a task, the
agent has to determine which model to use (if any) and then correctly
operate it by writing its own code. In the following, we describe how
our agents and tasks are implemented (see
[Fig. 1](#S3.F1 "In 3 Agent Evaluation and Benchmark Tasks ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")
for an overview).

Figure 1: Architecture of our agentic AI4S benchmark. The agent (center)
has access to different specialist models and is evaluated against their
published performance (right). By varying the axes of the agent’s
configuration within the same task (left), we can systematically study
its performance, reliability, and behavior under controlled, repeatable
conditions (bottom).

### 3.1 Modular Agent Implementation for Scientific Workflows

The agent runs in a sandbox with access to a single GPU and a pre-built
coding environment. The sandbox contains the weights and environments of
all specialist models, each with a short README that names the model and
links to its paper and code. Importantly, the specialist models are not
available through a dedicated tool call, but have to be operated by the
agent the same way a human scientist would. The agent receives a simple
system prompt that describes it as an “autonomous research agent”
([Section A.16](#A1.SS16 "A.16 Agent Prompt ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")).
It is then given the task description, the available data, and the
required solution format. It can read and write files, fetch web pages,
and run terminal commands, and can therefore write and execute its own
code.

In each step, the agent’s backbone model sees the conversation so far,
including the task description, all outputs, and every tool result.
Then, it either outputs plain text or calls one of the available tools
([Section A.2](#A1.SS2 "A.2 Tool Use and Specialist Model Usage ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")).
A tool’s output is appended to the conversation before the loop repeats,
so the agent always sees the outcome of its last action before choosing
its next one. The loop ends when the agent calls a finish tool with its
answer, or when the budget runs out. In its full form, this loop follows
[Yao et al. (2023)](#bib.bib6), interleaving reasoning about what to do
with the actions taken.

For our main analysis, we select and systematically vary five axes, each
targeting a distinct factor known to shape behavior. What agents are
told determines what they still need to explore or retrieve themselves
([Jimenez et al., 2024](#bib.bib47)). Keeping reasoning in context is
central to the performance gains of [Yao et al. (2023)](#bib.bib6), and
agents that check their own work tend to succeed more often ([Shinn et
al., 2023](#bib.bib48); [Madaan et al., 2023](#bib.bib49)). Giving
agents more time lets them solve harder problems, though with
diminishing returns ([Wijk et al., 2025](#bib.bib45); [Chan et al.,
2025](#bib.bib46)). Finally, the capability of the backbone model should
be evaluated separately from the harness built around it ([Kapoor et
al., 2025](#bib.bib1)). Together, the five axes cover what the agent
knows, how it deliberates, whether it checks itself, how much time it
has, and how capable it is, all of which can influence both outcome and
reliability. We describe the axes and their levels below. For
Information and Verification, each level adds to the previous one
(marked with +).

Information. This axis controls how much information the agent receives
in addition to the task description: (i) _none_: no additional
information; (ii) _identity_: which specialist model is associated with
the task; (iii) _interface_: + how to load and call the model; (iv)
_protocol_: + a full recipe for this specific task.

Reasoning. This axis controls whether the agent generates reasoning and
whether this reasoning stays in context for later steps: (i) _act-only_:
no reasoning is generated; (ii) _think-act_: reasoning is generated in
each step but discarded before the next; (iii) _ReAct_: reasoning is
generated and kept in context across steps.

Verification. This axis controls how strongly the prompt asks the agent
to verify its own answer: (i) _none_: no instruction to verify; (ii)
_asked_: the agent is asked to verify its answer; (iii) _reported_: +
the agent must state the score it expects and the evidence from its
verification; (iv) _binding_: + the agent is told not to submit unless
its own verification is convincing.

Budget. This axis controls how much wall-clock time the agent has to
solve the task. We limit runtime rather than the number of steps,
because the duration of a step varies widely (from a quick file read to
fine-tuning a specialist model): (i) _short_: 5 min; (ii) _medium_: 10
min; (iii) _long_: 20 min.

Model. This axis controls the size, and therefore the capability, of the
agent’s backbone model: (i) _small_: Qwen3.5-35B-A3B; (ii) _medium_:
Qwen3.5-122B-A10B; (iii) _large_: Qwen3.5-397B-A17B. All models are
FP8-quantized due to resource limitations.

### 3.2 Benchmark Tasks from Astrophysics and Genomics

To create the tasks, we identify published scientific works that propose
a new specialist model. For each, we reproduce the evaluation from the
original publication ourselves, reducing its size where necessary so
that it can be completed within the shortest budget (e.g., by
downsampling the evaluation dataset). The score of the specialist model
in our reproduction is the task’s reference score. Each task tests, in a
controlled setup, the agent’s ability to understand, reproduce, and use
prior work to complete a scientific workflow. We include the following
tasks
([Tables 1](#S3.T1 "In 3.2 Benchmark Tasks from Astrophysics and Genomics ‣ 3 Agent Evaluation and Benchmark Tasks ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")
and [A.17](#A1.SS17 "A.17 Specialist Model and Task Examples ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")):

redshift-estimation. The agent has to estimate the cosmological redshift
of galaxies directly from multi-band photometric images. Given 20 galaxy
image cutouts and a labeled reference set, it has to use the pretrained
AstroCLIP model ([Parker et al., 2024](#bib.bib8)) to predict continuous
redshift values. Performance is measured by $`R^{2}`$ against
spectroscopic ground-truth measurements.

mmlu-astronomy. This task consists of 152 multiple-choice questions on
topics from stellar evolution to cosmology. The specialist model,
AstroSage-8B ([de Haan et al., 2025](#bib.bib9)), is weaker than the
agent’s backbone model, so the task tests whether the agent recognizes
this and answers the questions itself instead of relying on the
specialist. Performance is measured by accuracy.

promoter-prediction. The agent has to classify 613 human DNA sequences
as promoter or non-promoter regions. To do so, it has to locate,
pre-process, fine-tune, and operate DNABERT-2 ([Zhou et al.,
2024](#bib.bib10)). Performance is measured by the Matthews correlation
coefficient (MCC).

rna-folding. The agent has to predict the secondary structures of 300
RNA sequences. It has to use the pretrained RiNALMo model ([Penić et
al., 2025](#bib.bib11)) to predict contacts between nucleotide pairs,
and then apply a post-processing procedure to obtain valid secondary
structures. Performance is measured by the structure-level pairing
$`F_{1}`$ score.

We distinguish two regimes: a task is gap_positive if the specialist’s
reference score is higher than the score of the backbone model alone
($`\mathcal{R}>\mathcal{B}`$), and gap_negative if it is lower. The four
tasks each stress a different part of using a specialist model
correctly. redshift-estimation and rna-folding reward finding a stronger
specialist and using it without fine-tuning, but the difficult step
differs (pre-processing input images before embedding them, and
post-processing the predicted contacts into valid structures).
promoter-prediction instead requires fine-tuning DNABERT-2, because its
pretrained checkpoint is not trained for promoter classification.
mmlu-astronomy is gap_negative: its specialist model has been surpassed
by general-purpose LLMs and is weaker than the backbone, so the correct
behavior is to decline the specialist rather than use it. With two
domains, two regimes, and four different demands on the specialist
model, no single fixed strategy (always use the model, or never use it)
performs well across all four tasks. To succeed, the agent has to
investigate and judge each specialist’s capabilities and work out its
specific operating details.

|            | redshift- estimation | mmlu- astronomy | promoter- prediction | rna-folding       |
| ---------- | -------------------- | --------------- | -------------------- | ----------------- |
| Domain     | Astrophysics         | Astrophysics    | Genomics             | Genomics          |
| Size       | 20 galaxy images     | 152 questions   | 613 DNA sequences    | 300 RNA sequences |
| Metric     | $`R^{2}`$            | Accuracy        | MCC                  | $`F_{1}`$         |
| Specialist | AstroCLIP            | AstroSage-8B    | DNABERT-2            | RiNALMo           |
| Challenge  | Pre-processing       | Declining       | Fine-tuning          | Post-processing   |
| Regime     | gap_positive         | gap_negative    | gap_positive         | gap_positive      |

Table 1: The four tasks of the benchmark, together with one example
instance per task. Each task belongs to one of two domains and one of
two regimes, and focuses on a different aspect of the specialist models’
operation.

## 4 Experiments and Results

### 4.1 Experimental Setup and Evaluation Metrics

To evaluate the agent, we use three quantities. $`\mathcal{B}`$ is the
score of the backbone model alone, i.e., the LLM answering the task
directly, without an agent or specialist model. $`\mathcal{R}`$ is the
reference score of the specialist model in our reproduction.
$`\mathcal{S}`$ is the agent’s score on the task. Our main metric is the
share of the gap between backbone and specialist that the agent closes
(gap_closed):

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\mathcal{G}=\frac{\mathcal{S}-\mathcal{B}}{\mathcal{R}-\mathcal{B}},
``` |  | (1) |

where $`\mathcal{G}=0`$ means no improvement over the backbone alone and
$`\mathcal{G}=1`$ means the agent matches the specialist’s reference
score. It is defined only for gap_positive tasks
($`\mathcal{R}>\mathcal{B}`$). A run *completes* if the agent submits an
answer with the finish tool before its budget runs out; runs that do not
complete receive no score. For every completed run, we also record a
binary *hurdle* indicator $`\mathcal{H}`$, which states whether the
run’s score exceeds the trivial score $`\mathcal{T}`$ of the task by
more than a margin $`\mu`$
([Section A.14](#A1.SS14 "A.14 Sensitivity to the Hurdle Margin ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")).
$`\mathcal{H}`$ thus captures whether a run makes a genuine attempt at
the task, and $`\mathcal{G}`$ captures how close it comes to the
reference. For each task, we evaluate the full grid over our axes: 4
(*Information*) $`\times`$ 3 (*Reasoning*) $`\times`$ 4 (*Verification*)
$`\times`$ 3 (*Budget*) $`\times`$ 3 (*Model*) $`=`$ 432 configurations,
which we call *cells*. To measure how much outcomes vary between runs,
we repeat every cell 5 times, which gives 2,160 runs per task and
$`4\times 2{,}160=8{,}640`$ runs in total for our main experiments.

### 4.2 Results

The four tasks differ widely in both score and reliability
([Table 2](#S4.T2 "In 4.2 Results ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")).
promoter-prediction is the most reliable: almost all of its completed
runs clear the hurdle, and repeated runs of the same configuration agree
closely. redshift-estimation is by far the least reliable, with more
than half of its completed runs failing to clear the hurdle. Unless
noted otherwise, the remaining analyses pool the three gap_positive
tasks, for which $`\mathcal{G}`$ is defined.

##### Agent outcomes are noisy.

Even among genuine attempts, about 54% of the score variance is
run-to-run noise rather than an effect of the configuration
([Fig. 2](#S4.F2 "In Agent outcomes are noisy. ‣ 4.2 Results ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation"),
right). Without excluding runs that fail the hurdle, the noise appears
even larger: differences between configurations then explain only 39.4%
of the variance, instead of 46.1%. This noise is not uniform: cells with
higher scores have systematically lower variance
([Fig. 2](#S4.F2 "In Agent outcomes are noisy. ‣ 4.2 Results ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation"),
left). Whether a run clears the hurdle at all is also inconsistent
across repeated runs, and this differs strongly between tasks: the
pooled outcome consistency is 0.86, but only 0.73 for
redshift-estimation, whose repeated runs disagree far more often than
those of the other tasks
([Tables 2](#S4.T2 "In 4.2 Results ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")
and [8](#A1.T8 "Table 8 ‣ A.3 Variance Decomposition and Hurdle ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")).
Even with 5 runs per cell, the 95% confidence interval of a cell’s mean
score remains wide
([Section A.3](#A1.SS3 "A.3 Variance Decomposition and Hurdle ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")).
Given the level of run-to-run noise and the uneven completion rates
across configurations and tasks, our results reinforce recent calls for
more rigorous reporting of completion rates, variance, and confidence
intervals alongside raw scores as standard practice in agent evaluations
([Kapoor et al., 2025](#bib.bib1); [Rabanser et al., 2026](#bib.bib2)).

Figure 2: Outcome variance across cells. Left: mean $`\mathcal{G}`$ vs.
SD per cell ($`\geq`$3 completed runs), with Spearman correlation.
Color: all/some/no runs clear the hurdle (green/orange/red). Right:
variance between vs. within cells, for all completed runs and
hurdle-clearing runs only.

##### Information has the largest axis effect.

We rank the five axes by effect size: the range of an axis’s mean
$`\mathcal{G}`$ across its levels, divided by the within-cell standard
deviation. *Information* has the largest effect on every task and
clearly outranks *Model*
([Table 3](#S4.T3 "In Information has the largest axis effect. ‣ 4.2 Results ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")).
On average, *Reasoning* matters more than *Budget*, and *Verification*
ranks last. Because the levels of an axis complete at different rates, a
ranking computed over completed runs can be affected by which runs
complete. The ranking is nevertheless robust: *Information* ranks first
in at least 99% of bootstrap samples, and a linear model gives the same
order
([Section A.9](#A1.SS9 "A.9 Uncertainty of the Axis Effects ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")).
This suggests that a user configuring an agent may benefit more from
prioritizing task information than from choosing a stronger backbone
model or a larger budget. The effect of one axis can, however, depend on
the others, which we examine next.

##### The effect of one axis depends on the others.

Increasing the *Budget* for the small and medium *Model* raises the
completion rate but lowers $`\mathcal{G}`$, while for the large *Model*
it raises both
([Fig. 3(a)](#S4.F3.sf1 "In Figure 3 ‣ The effect of one axis depends on the others. ‣ 4.2 Results ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")).
*Information* shows a similar pattern: at lower levels, more *Budget*
raises the completion rate without raising $`\mathcal{G}`$, while at the
*interface* level it raises both
([Fig. 6(a)](#A1.F6.sf1 "In Figure 6 ‣ A.5 Additional Interaction and Runtime Views ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")).
These patterns largely hold when we compare only configurations that
complete under every budget, and the largest interaction overall is
between *Information* and *Model*
([Sections A.10](#A1.SS10 "A.10 Interaction Effects and Non-Completion ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")
and [A.9](#A1.SS9 "A.9 Uncertainty of the Axis Effects ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")).
One explanation is that additional budget only improves the score once
the agent can use it productively, either because it knows what to do
(higher *Information*) or because it is capable enough (a larger
*Model*). Without either, more time may mainly let the agent continue an
unproductive approach until it submits, which would raise the completion
rate without raising the score. The redshift-estimation case study
matches this explanation: at the *none* level, more budget lowers the
score
([Table 9](#A1.T9 "In A.5 Additional Interaction and Runtime Views ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")).
One axis can therefore change not only how strongly another axis
matters, but also the direction of its effect, and whether it moves
completion and score in the same way. This supports evaluating agents as
configurable systems rather than fixed models: how the parts combine
matters as much as any single part.

(a) Interaction of the *Model* and *Budget* axes.

![Refer to
caption](2610.01618v1/cross_axis_effect_promoter+redshift+rna_information-cost-usd_v3.png)

(b) Axis effect of *Information* on task cost.

Figure 3: Left: $`\mathcal{G}`$ and number of completed runs per *Model*
and *Budget*; error bars show 95% CI of the mean. Right: distribution of
a run’s cost per *Information* level, colored by that level’s mean
$`\mathcal{G}`$. Additional plots are in
[Fig. 6](#A1.F6 "In A.5 Additional Interaction and Runtime Views ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation").

##### Axes affect more than completion and score.

Agents should be evaluated not only on their score but also on
accompanying metrics such as cost and runtime ([Kapoor et al.,
2025](#bib.bib1)). Lower *Information* levels not only reach a lower
$`\mathcal{G}`$, but also cost more and run longer
([Figs. 3(b)](#S4.F3.sf2 "In Figure 3 ‣ The effect of one axis depends on the others. ‣ 4.2 Results ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")
and [6(b)](#A1.F6.sf2 "Figure 6(b) ‣ Figure 6 ‣ A.5 Additional Interaction and Runtime Views ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")).
We also measure calibration error: the score the agent predicts for
itself minus its actual score, normalized by
$`|\mathcal{R}-\mathcal{B}|`$, so that positive values mean the agent
overestimates its result.²² 2 Agents report a predicted score only at
the *reported* and *binding* levels of *Verification*. On average,
agents are overconfident. *Reasoning* has virtually no effect on
calibration error, and the small model is more overconfident than the
medium and large models, which behave similarly. More *Information*
reduces the calibration error, most strongly at the *protocol* level,
where both its mean and its spread drop sharply
([Figs. 7](#A1.F7 "In A.6 Calibration Error ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")
and [A.6](#A1.SS6 "A.6 Calibration Error ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")).
*Information* therefore improves $`\mathcal{G}`$, lowers cost and
runtime, and improves calibration at the same time, with no trade-off,
making it worth the effort to provide.

##### Agents rarely decline a weaker specialist.

On the gap_negative task mmlu-astronomy, agents should answer with their
backbone instead of the weaker specialist. Yet 99.8% of runs use
AstroSage, including almost all runs at the *none* level, where it is
not mentioned, and the mean accuracy stays close to the specialist’s
([Section A.13](#A1.SS13 "A.13 Axis Analysis for mmlu-astronomy ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")).
Even with the oracle tool
([Section 4.3](#S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2 "Verification works better at the system level. ‣ 4.3 Ablations ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")),
which lets the agent check the accuracy of its answers, performance does
not increase substantially
([Table 12](#A1.T12 "In Model-family and open- vs. closed-weight ablations. ‣ A.8 Ablation Details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")).
Possible explanations are that agents assume a specialist model
outperforms a general one, similar to an authority bias ([Xie et al.,
2024](#bib.bib50)), or that they explore too little, e.g., by never
testing the backbone’s own answers. Investigating these is an
interesting direction for future work.

##### Summary.

Agent outcomes on long, specialized tasks are noisy: about 54% of the
score variance among genuine attempts is run-to-run noise rather than an
effect of the configuration, and completion and outcome consistency vary
sharply between tasks. A single run’s score is therefore not a reliable
signal on its own. Judging an axis only by its effect on $`\mathcal{G}`$
is also incomplete. *Information* has the largest effect on
$`\mathcal{G}`$, and at the same time lowers cost and runtime and
improves calibration. *Budget*, in contrast, mainly raises
$`\mathcal{G}`$ when the agent has enough information or a large enough
model to use the extra time productively. Agents also rarely question a
weaker specialist. Building and evaluating agents for such tasks should
therefore track completion, score, cost, runtime, and calibration
jointly across the axes that shape them, rather than optimizing a single
axis for a single metric.

### 4.3 Ablations

##### Different model families behave similarly, but are not interchangeable.

We rerun the experimental grid with an open-weight model from a
different family, Step-3.7-Flash (comparable to the medium Qwen model,
Qwen-122B), and with a closed model, Claude Sonnet 5 (roughly comparable
to the large Qwen model, Qwen-397B). Both open-weight models rank
*Information* first, while the order of the other axes shifts slightly
([Table 14](#A1.T14 "In Model-family and open- vs. closed-weight ablations. ‣ A.8 Ablation Details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")).
Step-3.7-Flash also reaches a higher $`\mathcal{G}`$ than Qwen-122B at
about half the cost per run
([Table 15](#A1.T15 "In Model-family and open- vs. closed-weight ablations. ‣ A.8 Ablation Details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")).
The comparison between open-weight and closed model shows a sharper
difference. The order of the other axes stays the same, but *Budget*
rises from third to first rank for Sonnet 5
([Table 16](#A1.T16 "In Model-family and open- vs. closed-weight ablations. ‣ A.8 Ablation Details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")).
*Information* still matters, but less than time: the closed model is
markedly more sensitive to how long it runs than to how much it is told.
Sonnet 5 also executes far more efficiently: pooled across tasks, it
needs less than half the tool calls of Qwen-397B, produces about a fifth
of the tool-call errors, and is better calibrated. Yet at list prices,
it costs more, and its pooled $`\mathcal{G}`$ is lower
([Table 17](#A1.T17 "In Model-family and open- vs. closed-weight ablations. ‣ A.8 Ablation Details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")).
Efficient, low-error execution thus does not by itself lead to a better
outcome, analogous to the decoupling of capability and reliability
described by [Rabanser et al. (2026)](#bib.bib2). A system tuned to one
model’s characteristics therefore does not automatically transfer to
another, necessitating a systematic analysis like ours to inform the
system’s priorities.

##### Verification works better at the system level.

The *Verification* axis only prompts the agent to check its own work, as
a user would, and its effect ranks last among all five axes
([Table 3](#S4.T3 "In Information has the largest axis effect. ‣ 4.2 Results ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")).
To test whether verification works better when it is provided by the
system instead, we equip the agent with an *oracle* tool that it can
call at any point to score its current submission against the task’s
reference solution. The oracle represents the strongest form of
system-level verification; in practice, a system would offer weaker
checks, such as a validation set. We rerun the full grid with the oracle
for two models, Qwen-122B and Step-3.7-Flash, with all axes varied as in
the main experiments
([Table 12](#A1.T12 "In Model-family and open- vs. closed-weight ablations. ‣ A.8 Ablation Details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")).
The oracle raises the score for both models on every task. It also
sharply reduces the calibration error, which the prompted *Verification*
axis does not. These gains are not free: runtime and cost rise in every
case, because the agent makes more tool calls. Since the agent could
also use the oracle to search for the correct answer, we checked all
oracle runs for such hill-climbing. It occurs in only 4.4% of runs, and
excluding them barely changes the results
([Section A.12](#A1.SS12 "A.12 Use of the Oracle Tool ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")).
This indicates that some agent behaviors, and the outcomes that depend
on them, are easier to influence through the system than through the
user’s prompt.

## 5 Analysis: Taxonomy of Agent Behavior

Scores show whether an agent succeeds, but not how it behaves or why it
fails. To study this, we automatically extract and classify the agents’
outcomes and the behaviors that lead to them from the trajectories,
using the following pipeline:

##### Stage 1: Structured Per-Trajectory Extraction.

For every trajectory, we prompt a judge model, DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731,
to describe the trajectory along six dimensions: (i) an overall result
characterization, (ii) the single root error category when applicable,
(iii) specialist model usage, (iv) verification behavior, (v) planning
and exploration, and (vi) execution quality. For every dimension, the
judge receives the same context: the task description, the complete
trajectory log, automatically derived facts about model usage and
scoring, the task’s intended solution approach, and the agent’s final
workspace. Following the extract-then-cluster method of [Chirkova et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib7), each dimension is extracted as domain-agnostic free
text rather than assigned from a predefined set of labels. The prompts
are in
[Section A.18](#A1.SS18 "A.18 Taxonomy Prompts ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation").

##### Stage 2: Clustering and Category Induction.

We then consolidate the free-text descriptions of each dimension into a
small set of general behavioral categories in three steps. First, we
embed the descriptions with a Sentence-BERT model and cluster them with
HDBSCAN; points that HDBSCAN leaves unassigned are added to their most
similar cluster. Second, the judge model labels each cluster with a
short, general description of the behavior, based on a representative
sample of its members. Task-specific details go into a separate
criterion rather than into the label. Third, the judge model reviews all
cluster labels of one dimension at once and merges them into at most
$`K=8`$ general categories, combining near-duplicates and overly
specific labels. In practice, no dimension reached this limit. As a
result, every trajectory receives one category per dimension, which we
cross-tabulate against the experimental conditions (details in
[Section A.15](#A1.SS15 "A.15 Taxonomy Results ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")).

##### Results.

Figure 4: Distribution of verification behavior categories per level of
the *Verification* axis, without (Baseline) and with the *oracle* tool,
pooled across Qwen-122B, Step-3.7-Flash, and all tasks.

Across all dimensions, *Information* has the strongest association with
the distribution of categories
([Table 24](#A1.T24 "In A.15 Taxonomy Results ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")),
consistent with its dominant effect on scores. We highlight one case
study that connects to the previous section: *verification behavior*.
The prompted *Verification* axis had the smallest effect on the score
([Table 3](#S4.T3 "In Information has the largest axis effect. ‣ 4.2 Results ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")),
while the oracle tool raised the score for both models on every task
([Section 4.3](#S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2 "Verification works better at the system level. ‣ 4.3 Ablations ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")).
The taxonomy shows how the agents’ behavior differs between the two.
Without the oracle, prompting barely changes how agents verify: from
*none* to *binding*, the share of reference-based verification rises
only from 19% to 22%, and about three quarters of runs check only the
format of their answer
([Fig. 4](#S5.F4 "In Results. ‣ 5 Analysis: Taxonomy of Agent Behavior ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")).
With the oracle, the share of reference-based verification roughly
triples at every prompt level. Part of this shift reflects the oracle
calls themselves, but it shows that agents use a verification option
when the system offers one, largely regardless of what the prompt asks
for. This illustrates a broader point: some agent behaviors are hard to
shift through the user’s prompt but respond strongly to what the system
provides, and the system should be designed with this distinction in
mind.

## 6 Conclusion

We systematically study how five axes of an agent’s configuration
influence its outcomes on scientific tasks that require operating
specialist models. Four findings stand out. First, agent outcomes are
noisy: about 54% of the score variance among genuine attempts is
run-to-run noise rather than an effect of the configuration. Second, in
our main experiments, the information given to the agent has the largest
effect on the score, outranking both the backbone model and the budget,
and it also lowers cost and runtime and improves calibration. Third,
axes interact: additional budget mainly raises the score when the agent
has enough information or a large enough model to use it productively,
and can lower the score otherwise, so axes cannot be tuned in isolation.
Fourth, some agent behaviors, such as self-verification, barely respond
to prompting by the user but shift strongly when the system provides a
dedicated tool. Together, these results argue for evaluating and
building agents as configurable systems rather than fixed models:
tracking completion, variance, cost, and calibration alongside raw
scores, and designing the system around behaviors that prompting alone
cannot reliably control.

##### Limitations.

Our analysis covers over 18,000 agent trajectories, but is limited to
four tasks across two scientific domains. More tasks and domains would
strengthen the generality of the conclusions. We exclude several further
system components (memory, multi-agent coordination) that future work
should vary as additional axes. Finally, our finding that some agent
behaviors respond more to system-level design than to user prompting is
demonstrated on one dimension (verification) and needs to be tested
across other behavioral dimensions before it can be treated as a general
principle.

### AI use statement

In this work, we used generative AI tools to propose or refine
hypotheses, design or provide feedback on research methodology or
experiments, implement methods, support qualitative and thematic data
analysis, and interpret results. We have not used generative AI tools
(or it is not applicable to this work) to generate synthetic data sets,
help develop theoretical models or conceptual frameworks, formulate
mathematical claims, provide critical ingredients for proving
mathematical claims or assist in the writing of proofs. Additionally, we
used generative AI tools to create or modify scientific figures or
images, suggest experimental parameters, create or edit software code,
draft parts of a research paper, summarize or analyse existing
literature, discover research topics or identify gaps, brainstorming,
sourcing/searching for information, identify relevant literature, and
propose a title or keywords for a research paper. We have reviewed all
AI-assisted work. All AI use was exclusively used as a first step, and
went through manual checks for accuracy, correctness, potential
plagiarism, and understandability. We take responsibility for the final
content of this work, including text, claims or artifacts produced with
the aid of generative AI.

### Reproducibility statement

To make the paper fully reproducible, we will release all code and
instructions on how to use it. We will additionally release all produced
artifacts (agent traces) and derived analyses (raw taxonomy data) to
encourage further usage in the community.

## Appendix A Appendix

### A.1 Implementation Details

We serve each open-weight model with vLLM, using tensor parallelism
across its GPUs: one NVIDIA H100 GPU for the small Qwen model, two for
the medium, eight for the large, and four for Step-3.7-Flash. All models
are FP8-quantized and use a context window of 262,144 (Qwen) or 256,000
(Step) tokens. Claude Sonnet 5 is accessed through the Anthropic API.
Each cell runs as a separate SLURM array job against the shared model
server, with up to 8 concurrent agent runs, each in its own sandbox with
access to a single GPU.
[Table 4](#A1.T4 "In A.1 Implementation Details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")
lists the composition of the released trajectories.

| Grid | Cells per task | Runs per task | Trajectories |
|----|----|----|----|
| Main experiments (3 Qwen3.5 models) | 432 | 2,160 | 8,640 |
| Step-3.7-Flash (no *act-only*) | 96 | 480 | 1,920 |
| Claude Sonnet 5 | 144 | 720 | 2,880 |
| Oracle, Qwen-122B | 144 | 720 | 2,880 |
| Oracle, Step-3.7-Flash | 96 | 480 | 1,920 |
| Total |  |  | 18,240 |

Table 4: Composition of the released trajectories. Each cell is repeated
5 times and the grid covers all four tasks.

### A.3 Variance Decomposition and Hurdle

|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|

| mmlu-astronomy | 4.7% \[3.9, 5.7\] | 0.905 | 29.4% | 6.9% | 17.6% | 20.8% |
| promoter-prediction | 0.5% \[0.2, 0.9\] | 0.986 | 47.9% | 49.7% | 10.7% | 12.9% |
| rna-folding | 8.7% \[7.3, 10.3\] | 0.825 | 45.7% | 35.2% | 12.8% | 13.0% |
| Pooled (3 gap_positive tasks, task means removed) | 20.6% \[19.5, 21.7\] | 0.858 | 39.4% | 46.1% | — | — |

Table 8: Hurdle decomposition and run-to-run variance per task. Mean
per-cell SD and the 95% CI half-width of a cell’s mean score (at 5 runs)
are expressed as % of $`|\mathcal{R}-\mathcal{T}|`$, so they are
comparable across tasks. The pooled CI half-width in units of
$`\mathcal{G}`$ is shown in
[Fig. 5](#A1.F5 "In A.4 Additional Completion Analyses ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")
(right).

##### Intraclass correlation.

To separate real signal between configurations from run-to-run noise, we
decompose the score variance in two steps. First, a one-way
random-effects ANOVA over all cells with at least three completed runs
splits the total variance into a within-cell component
($`MS_{\text{within}}`$) and a bias-corrected between-cell component.
From these, we compute the intraclass correlation

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\text{ICC}=\frac{\sigma^{2}_{\text{between}}}{\sigma^{2}_{\text{between}}+\sigma^{2}_{\text{within}}},
``` |  |

the share of the total variance that comes from differences between
cells rather than from run-to-run noise. On its own, this decomposition
is misleading: a run can complete and still fail to make a genuine
attempt at the task (e.g., by running the wrong specialist model or
submitting predictions far below the trivial score). Because the ANOVA
sums squared deviations, such rare but severe failures inflate
$`MS_{\text{within}}`$ far out of proportion to how often they occur. We
therefore also compute a two-part (hurdle) decomposition ([Cragg,
1971](#bib.bib17)), following recent work on the reliability of LLM
agents across repeated trials that separates a binary success indicator
per run from a continuous score given success ([Rabanser et al.,
2026](#bib.bib2); [Khanal et al., 2026](#bib.bib18)).

##### Hurdle indicator and failure rate.

We write $`y\in\{0,1\}`$ for the hurdle indicator $`\mathcal{H}`$ of a
run: $`y=1`$ if the run’s score exceeds the trivial score
$`\mathcal{T}`$ by more than the margin $`\mu`$, and $`y=0`$ otherwise.
The hurdle is distinct from completion: runs that do not complete (e.g.,
because they run out of budget) have no score and are not counted here
at all. The *hurdle failure rate* is the share of completed runs with
$`y=0`$, i.e., $`1-\bar{y}`$. We report 95% Wilson score
intervals ([Wilson, 1927](#bib.bib19)). The completion rate in
[Table 2](#S4.T2 "In 4.2 Results ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")
uses the same interval, computed over all 2,160 runs of a task. The
$`\pm`$ values in
[Table 2](#S4.T2 "In 4.2 Results ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")
give the half-widths of these intervals, which are nearly symmetric at
these sample sizes.

##### Outcome consistency.

For each cell $`i`$ with at least 3 completed runs, let $`\hat{p}_{i}`$
be the share of its runs that clear the hurdle. Following [Rabanser et
al. (2026)](#bib.bib2),

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
C_{\text{out}}=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k}(2\hat{p}_{i}-1)^{2}=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\left[1-\frac{\hat{p}_{i}(1-\hat{p}_{i})}{0.25}\right],
``` |  |

averaged over the $`k`$ qualifying cells. Each term normalizes the
variance of the cell’s binary outcomes by the maximum variance of a
Bernoulli variable, 0.25. A cell contributes 1 if all its runs clear the
hurdle or all fail it, and 0 if exactly half of them clear it.
$`C_{\text{out}}=1`$ therefore means that every configuration reliably
succeeds or reliably fails.

##### Variance among genuine attempts.

We apply the same ANOVA and ICC to runs with $`y=1`$ only. This measures
how repeatable an agent’s score is, given that it makes a genuine
attempt. Since this restriction selects runs by their outcome, it can
bias the variance estimate, so we report both versions.

##### Pooling across tasks.

Cells are defined per task. Pooling the raw $`\mathcal{G}`$ values of
several tasks would therefore count differences between the task means
as differences between cells, and inflate the pooled ICC above every
per-task value. We therefore subtract each task’s mean before pooling.

### A.4 Additional Completion Analyses

Not every run produces a score, for example when the agent runs out of
budget before submitting a solution. Across all four tasks, 80.7% of
runs complete, and 19.3% run out of budget. Completion also varies
within configurations: on every task, a substantial share of cells
completes on some runs but not on others, from run-to-run variation
alone
([Table 2](#S4.T2 "In 4.2 Results ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation");
[Fig. 5](#A1.F5 "In A.4 Additional Completion Analyses ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation"),
left, for the three gap_positive tasks). Per-cell completion rates range
from 0% to 100% on every task except mmlu-astronomy, where every
configuration completes at least 20% of its runs. We flag a run as an
extreme outlier if its score differs from the trivial score by more than
10 times the gap between reference and trivial score,
$`10\,|\mathcal{R}-\mathcal{T}|`$. Such outliers occur only on
redshift-estimation (7 of 1,647 completed runs, 0.4%), all but one with
the small model. We exclude them from all score-based analyses.

##### Case study: redshift-estimation.

How axes interact depends on the task, but redshift-estimation offers a
clear example
([Table 9](#A1.T9 "In A.5 Additional Interaction and Runtime Views ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")).
At the *none* level, more *Budget* lowers the score
($`-0.429\to-0.713`$) at similar hurdle failure rates, consistent with
the agent pursuing a wrong approach further. At the *interface* level,
more *Budget* raises the score ($`-0.605\to-0.380`$) and lowers the
hurdle failure rate: the agent now knows enough to use the extra time.
At the *protocol* level, *Budget* makes no difference, because every run
already reproduces the reference score. The medians show the same
pattern (*none*: $`-0.34\to-0.50`$; *interface*: $`-0.55\to-0.34`$), and
so does the comparison restricted to configurations that have completed
runs under all three budgets (*none*: $`-0.44\to-0.77`$; *interface*:
$`-0.61\to-0.38`$).

### A.9 Uncertainty of the Axis Effects

The effect size in
[Table 3](#S4.T3 "In Information has the largest axis effect. ‣ 4.2 Results ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")
carries no uncertainty on its own. We complement it in two ways. First,
we bootstrap the ranking: in each of 1,000 draws, we resample the runs
within every cell with replacement (runs that do not complete stay
incomplete), recompute all effect sizes, and record which axis ranks
first. Second, we fit a linear model to $`\mathcal{G}`$ of the completed
runs of each task, with all five axes as categorical factors (and, for
the interactions, all two-way interactions). We report partial
$`\eta^{2}`$, the share of the variance that an axis explains after
accounting for the other axes, with 95% intervals from 200 bootstrap
draws. *Information* ranks first on every task in at least 99% of the
draws, and partial $`\eta^{2}`$ gives the same order as the effect size,
except that *Budget* drops behind *Reasoning*, *Model*, and
*Verification* on redshift-estimation. Among the two-way interactions,
*Information*$`\times`$*Model* is the largest on promoter-prediction
($`F=12.4`$, $`p<10^{-12}`$, partial $`\eta^{2}=0.04`$) and rna-folding
($`F=32.1`$, $`p<10^{-35}`$, partial $`\eta^{2}=0.13`$).
*Budget*$`\times`$*Model* is significant on rna-folding ($`p<10^{-3}`$)
but not on the other two tasks ($`p=0.08`$ and $`p=0.36`$), and
*Information*$`\times`$*Budget* is significant on promoter-prediction
($`p=0.002`$), borderline on redshift-estimation ($`p=0.055`$) and not
significant on rna-folding ($`p=0.18`$).

### A.10 Interaction Effects and Non-Completion

Scores are observed only for runs that complete, and completion itself
depends on the *Budget*. A drop in the mean score with more budget could
therefore come from weaker runs that now complete, rather than from runs
becoming worse. We test this in two ways. First, we restrict the
comparison to *matched* configurations, i.e., settings of all axes
except *Budget* that produce at least $`k`$ completed runs under every
budget level. Second, we report medians next to means. Confidence
intervals come from a bootstrap that resamples runs within each cell
(1,000 draws). The interactions in
[Section 4](#S4 "4 Experiments and Results ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")
largely hold under these checks
([Table 19](#A1.T19 "In A.10 Interaction Effects and Non-Completion ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")).
For the small model (Qwen-35B), the mean and median $`\mathcal{G}`$
still fall with more budget in matched configurations, and for the large
model (Qwen-397B) they rise. The drop for the small model disappears
only under the strictest matching (at least three completed runs per
budget level: mean $`\mathcal{G}`$ of 0.81 at *short* and 0.82 at
*long*), so part of it is a selection effect. At the *interface* level
of *Information*, more budget raises both mean and median. At *none* and
*identity*, the mean does not change; at *none*, the median rises
slightly.

### A.11 Generation Speed and Tool Time

Because the *Budget* is wall-clock time, a faster model gets more done
within the same budget.
[Table 20](#A1.T20 "In A.11 Generation Speed and Tool Time ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")
reports, per model, how the wall-clock time of a run splits into LLM
generation and tool execution, how many steps a model takes per minute,
and how fast it generates. We derive these numbers from the time stamps
in the trajectories: the time before an LLM response is counted as
generation time, and the time before a tool result as tool time. Tool
execution, not generation, takes most of the wall-clock time for every
model (54–73%), so the budget mostly limits how much code the agent can
run. The three Qwen models take a similar number of steps per minute
(6.0–7.2), because the smaller model’s faster generation is spent on
more and shorter steps; between the *short* and *long* budget, the
median number of steps per run grows from 25 to 36 for Qwen-35B and from
18 to 24 for the two larger models. Claude Sonnet 5 takes fewer steps
per minute than the open models and spends a larger share of its time
executing code, so its stronger sensitivity to the budget is not
explained by faster inference. The speed of generation varied only
moderately across runs (CV 0.16–0.26), both on our shared model server
and through the Anthropic API.

| Model           | LLM s / step | Steps / min | Tokens / s | CV   | LLM share | Tool share |
|-----------------|--------------|-------------|------------|------|-----------|------------|
| Qwen-35B        | 2.4          | 7.2         | 127        | 0.26 | 30%       | 70%        |
| Qwen-122B       | 4.1          | 6.0         | 83         | 0.16 | 41%       | 59%        |
| Qwen-397B       | 4.5          | 6.1         | 70         | 0.24 | 45%       | 55%        |
| Step-3.7-Flash  | 4.3          | 6.0         | 94         | 0.18 | 46%       | 54%        |
| Claude Sonnet 5 | 4.6          | 3.6         | 84         | 0.16 | 27%       | 73%        |

Table 20: Generation speed and use of time per model, medians over all
runs of the respective grid. Steps are LLM calls; LLM s / step is the
generation time per step. CV is the coefficient of variation of the
generation speed across runs.

### A.12 Use of the Oracle Tool

Since the oracle scores a submission against the test labels, an agent
could use it to search for the correct answer instead of verifying its
approach.
[Table 21](#A1.T21 "In A.12 Use of the Oracle Tool ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")
shows how often agents called it. Most runs call it rarely, but 8–22% of
runs call it five times or more. We flag a run as likely hill-climbing
when it calls the oracle at least five times and at least half of the
repeated calls follow only file edits, without re-running any code in
between. This applies to 4.4% of all oracle runs (210 of 4,800), mostly
on redshift-estimation (10–15% of its runs), where the most extreme runs
call the oracle up to 111 times while tuning the regression step. On
mmlu-astronomy, where changing single answers would be the most direct
form of search, we find almost no such runs (0.1–1.5%). Excluding
flagged runs barely changes the pooled $`\mathcal{G}`$ with the oracle
(Qwen-122B: 0.923 to 0.922; Step-3.7-Flash: 0.889 to 0.878), which stays
above the baseline without the oracle (0.822 and 0.865).

| Model | Task | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3–4 | $`\geq`$5 | Mean calls | Flagged |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Qwen-122B | redshift-estimation | 19.7% | 38.9% | 8.3% | 11.7% | 21.4% | 4.6 | 9.7% |
|  | mmlu-astronomy | 8.1% | 68.3% | 8.3% | 7.5% | 7.8% | 1.7 | 0.1% |
|  | promoter-prediction | 3.8% | 44.9% | 11.0% | 18.9% | 21.5% | 3.0 | 2.5% |
|  | rna-folding | 27.8% | 44.6% | 9.4% | 9.2% | 9.0% | 1.7 | 2.8% |
| Step-3.7-Flash | redshift-estimation | 44.6% | 25.8% | 4.8% | 5.6% | 19.2% | 4.0 | 14.6% |
|  | mmlu-astronomy | 34.6% | 25.2% | 12.3% | 14.6% | 13.3% | 2.0 | 1.5% |
|  | promoter-prediction | 37.5% | 24.0% | 7.9% | 11.2% | 19.4% | 2.2 | 1.0% |
|  | rna-folding | 49.4% | 27.9% | 7.9% | 5.4% | 9.4% | 1.9 | 4.0% |

Table 21: Number of oracle_check calls per run (share of runs) and share
of runs flagged as likely hill-climbing.

### A.13 Axis Analysis for mmlu-astronomy

$`\mathcal{G}`$ is not comparable between the two regimes, so we analyze
mmlu-astronomy on raw accuracy
([Table 22](#A1.T22 "In A.13 Axis Analysis for mmlu-astronomy ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")).
The correct behavior on this task is to answer with the backbone and
decline AstroSage, but agents almost never do this. The model-usage
heuristic in
[Table 7](#A1.T7 "In A.2 Tool Use and Specialist Model Usage ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")
counts only commands that name the model’s path and finds that AstroSage
was executed in 66% of runs; if we also count scripts that load
AstroSage and are then executed, 99.8% of all runs used it. This
explains why accuracy (0.685 on average) stays close to AstroSage’s own
reference accuracy (0.671) and far below the backbone alone (0.967).
Ranked by the same effect size as in
[Table 3](#S4.T3 "In Information has the largest axis effect. ‣ 4.2 Results ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation"),
*Information* (0.93) and *Model* (0.87) matter most, followed by
*Budget* (0.15), *Reasoning* (0.08) and *Verification* (0.05). The
*protocol* level, which describes how to run AstroSage, lowers accuracy
from about 0.71 to 0.62, presumably because it describes the weaker
specialist in the most detail and thus points the agent further toward
it.

| Axis          | Level     | Completion | Mean accuracy |
|---------------|-----------|------------|---------------|
| *Information* | none      | 92.8%      | 0.699         |
|               | identity  | 93.9%      | 0.712         |
|               | interface | 98.7%      | 0.710         |
|               | protocol  | 95.7%      | 0.617         |
| *Model*       | Qwen-35B  | 89.6%      | 0.626         |
|               | Qwen-122B | 97.5%      | 0.707         |
|               | Qwen-397B | 98.8%      | 0.715         |

Table 22: mmlu-astronomy: completion rate and mean accuracy per level of
*Information* and *Model*. Backbone alone: 0.967; AstroSage reference:
0.671; chance: 0.25.

### A.14 Sensitivity to the Hurdle Margin

The margin $`\mu`$ decides when a run counts as clearing the hurdle. We
set $`\mu`$ per task from the sampling noise of its metric.
[Table 23](#A1.T23 "In A.14 Sensitivity to the Hurdle Margin ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")
repeats the hurdle statistics with $`\mu`$ set at 0, 0.5, 1, and 2 times
its default value per task. The results change little, except in two
places. With $`\mu=0`$ on rna-folding, almost every run clears the
hurdle, because its trivial score is 0 and nearly every completed run
scores above 0. On redshift-estimation, doubling $`\mu`$ (a threshold of
$`R^{2}>0.5`$) removes the weakest hurdle-clearing runs, which raises
its ICC. The pooled ICC stays between 45% and 47% for every value.

|  | Hurdle failure rate |  |  |  | ICC, hurdle-clearing |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Task | $`0\mu`$ | $`0.5\mu`$ | $`1\mu`$ | $`2\mu`$ | $`0\mu`$ | $`0.5\mu`$ | $`1\mu`$ | $`2\mu`$ |
| redshift-estimation | 48.7% | 53.4% | 53.8% | 54.1% | 35.8% | 36.2% | 36.2% | 53.3% |
| mmlu-astronomy | 4.2% | 4.3% | 4.7% | 5.5% | 6.9% | 7.1% | 6.9% | 7.2% |
| promoter-prediction | 0.2% | 0.3% | 0.5% | 0.6% | 48.7% | 48.7% | 49.7% | 50.0% |
| rna-folding | 0.2% | 7.5% | 8.7% | 9.5% | 45.8% | 35.7% | 35.2% | 34.2% |
| Pooled | 16.4% | 20.0% | 20.6% | 20.9% | 47.4% | 44.8% | 46.1% | 46.4% |

Table 23: Hurdle failure rate and ICC among hurdle-clearing runs for
different multiples of the default margin $`\mu`$. Pooled: three
gap_positive tasks, task means removed.

### A.15 Taxonomy Results

[Table 24](#A1.T24 "In A.15 Taxonomy Results ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Agents are systems, not models: Rethinking agentic evaluation")
shows how strongly each axis is associated with the category
distribution of each taxonomy dimension, measured by Cramér’s V.
*Information* ranks first on all six dimensions, consistent with its
dominant effect on scores. *Model* and *Budget* show moderate
associations, particularly with error categories and results, while
*Reasoning* and *Verification* are only weakly associated with every
dimension.
````
